Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) -- Iraq's government has authorized Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki to submit to Washington amendments to a draft security agreement with the United States, an Iraqi government spokesman said Tuesday. Students protest the status-of-forces agreement Tuesday at Baghdad's Mustansiriya University. Ali al-Dabbagh said the Iraqi government approved several amendments that were "necessary, essential and appropriate" to the draft status-of-forces agreement, which would set the terms for U.S. troops in Iraq after the United Nations mandate on their presence expires at the end of this year. "The Iraqi government authorizes the prime minister to bring up these amendments to the U.S. side in order to reach a draft agreement that will preserve the fundamental principles and the sovereignty of Iraq and its high interests," al-Dabbagh said. It is unclear when al-Maliki will submit the changes to the draft document. U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates recently said that there was "great reluctance" to make any more changes to the agreement. However, senior U.S. officials -- speaking under the condition of anonymity -- are not ruling out possibly renegotiating parts of the deal with Iraq if the country's parliament does not approve it. The most vocal opponent of the draft security deal in Iraq has been the political party of radical Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, which opposes any U.S. military presence in Iraq. U.S. military helicopters Tuesday flew over Baghdad's Mustansiriya University, where hundreds of students took part in a demonstration organized by the Sadr movement against the status-of-forces deal. "We are against this agreement between the Iraqi government and between the American government because it is against Iraqi sovereignty," said law student Ahmed Fadhil Abbas, one of the demonstrators. Fellow demonstrator and law student Hisham Mohammed said the students plan to organize a sit-in and a strike across universities in Iraq to protest the agreement. The draft status-of-forces agreement, according to a copy obtained by CNN, calls for U.S. combat troops to be out of Iraqi cities and villages by July 30, 2009, and out of the country entirely by December 31, 2011. The agreement allows for an earlier withdrawal or an extension of the U.S. forces' stay in Iraq, by agreement of both parties. It also allows the Iraqi government to ask "the United States government to leave certain forces for training and for support purposes for the Iraqi forces." Legal jurisdiction over U.S. forces in Iraq has been a sticking point in the negotiation, with the U.S. side preferring that its troops and contractors remain immune from Iraqi law. Baghdad had sought the power to arrest and try Americans accused of crimes not related to official military operations, plus jurisdiction over troops and contractors who commit major crimes in the course of their duties. Under the draft agreement, U.S. forces or contractors who commit "major and premeditated murders" while off duty and outside U.S. facilities would fall under Iraqi jurisdiction, according to the copy obtained by CNN. All other crimes -- and murders committed inside U.S. facilities or by on-duty forces -- would fall under American jurisdiction, the agreement says.

BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) -- On Tuesday, an Iraqi government spokesman announced that officials in Baghdad have given Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki the green light to present proposed revisions to a draft security pact with the United States. That same day, students at Baghdad's Mustansiriya University staged a protest against the status-of-forces agreement.

According to spokesman Ali al-Dabbagh, the Iraqi government signed off on a number of changes it deemed "necessary, essential and appropriate" to the proposed status-of-forces agreement. This document would establish the rules governing American forces in Iraq once the United Nations mandate covering their deployment runs out at the close of this year.

"The Iraqi government authorizes the prime minister to bring up these amendments to the U.S. side in order to reach a draft agreement that will preserve the fundamental principles and the sovereignty of Iraq and its high interests," al-Dabbagh stated.

Exactly when al-Maliki intends to hand over the proposed revisions remains uncertain. Not long ago, U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates indicated there was "great reluctance" toward altering the pact any further. Even so, unnamed senior American officials have not dismissed the possibility of reopening talks on certain elements of the arrangement should Iraq's parliament fail to ratify it.

Within Iraq, the loudest resistance to the proposed security pact has come from the political movement led by firebrand Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, which rejects any American military footprint in the country. On Tuesday, U.S. military helicopters passed above Mustansiriya University in Baghdad, where hundreds of students gathered for a Sadr-organized rally opposing the status-of-forces deal.

"We are against this agreement between the Iraqi government and between the American government because it is against Iraqi sovereignty," declared Ahmed Fadhil Abbas, a law student among the protesters. Hisham Mohammed, another law student taking part, said students intend to launch a sit-in and a walkout at universities throughout Iraq to voice their opposition to the deal.

A copy of the draft status-of-forces agreement reviewed by CNN specifies that American combat forces must withdraw from Iraqi cities and villages by July 30, 2009, and depart the country completely by December 31, 2011. The pact permits either a quicker pullout or a longer stay for U.S. troops, provided both sides consent. It further grants the Iraqi government the option to request that "the United States government leave certain forces for training and for support purposes for the Iraqi forces."

The question of who holds legal authority over U.S. personnel in Iraq has proven a major obstacle in the talks, as Washington has favored keeping its soldiers and contractors shielded from Iraqi law. Baghdad, meanwhile, wanted the ability to detain and prosecute Americans charged with offenses unconnected to official military duties, as well as authority over troops and contractors who commit serious crimes while carrying out their assignments.

Per the copy obtained by CNN, the draft agreement places U.S. troops or contractors who commit "major and premeditated murders" while off duty and away from American installations under Iraqi legal authority. Every other offense -- including killings that take place within U.S. facilities or are carried out by personnel on duty -- would remain under American jurisdiction, the document states.

# Iraqi Cabinet Authorizes Maliki to Seek Changes to U.S. Security Pact

**BAGHDAD** — Iraq's cabinet on Tuesday authorized Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki to submit proposed amendments to a draft security agreement with the United States, as negotiations over the future of American forces in the country entered a critical phase.

The move reflects mounting political pressure within Iraq over the terms of the status-of-forces agreement, which would provide the legal framework for the continued presence of U.S. troops after the United Nations mandate authorizing their deployment expires at the end of the year.

## Terms of the Agreement

The draft agreement, hammered out over months of difficult negotiations, includes several key provisions that have generated intense debate among Iraqi lawmakers and the broader public.

Under the proposed terms, U.S. combat forces would withdraw from Iraqi cities, villages, and towns by the summer of 2009, with a complete withdrawal of American troops from Iraqi territory by the end of 2011. The timetable represents a significant point for Iraqi negotiators, who pushed for firm dates rather than conditions-based benchmarks.

The agreement also addresses the contentious issue of legal jurisdiction over American personnel. Under certain circumstances, U.S. troops and contractors could be subject to Iraqi law for serious crimes committed off-duty and off-base — a provision that American officials had resisted but ultimately accepted in modified form.

Other provisions would require U.S. forces to obtain Iraqi approval for military operations and would bar the United States from using Iraqi territory as a launching point for attacks on neighboring countries.

## Political Divisions and Protests

The proposed pact has exposed deep divisions within Iraq's political landscape. Supporters argue the agreement provides needed stability and a clear framework for the eventual restoration of full Iraqi sovereignty. Critics contend it concedes too much to American interests.

Followers of the influential Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr have been among the most vocal opponents of the agreement. Sadrist demonstrators have repeatedly taken to the streets of Baghdad and other cities to voice their opposition, denouncing what they characterize as an infringement on Iraqi independence.

Student demonstrations have added to the pressure on the government, with young protesters organizing rallies to reject any long-term American military presence. The protesters have called for a complete and immediate withdrawal of foreign forces, reflecting a broader current of nationalist sentiment that has complicated the government's efforts to build consensus.

## The Road Ahead

Any amendments proposed by Baghdad would need to be reviewed by American officials, raising questions about whether the agreement can be finalized before the year-end deadline. U.S. officials have indicated a willingness to consider Iraqi concerns but have cautioned that reopening core provisions could jeopardize the delicate compromise.

If approved, the agreement would still require ratification by Iraq's parliament, where the various political blocs remain divided over its terms.

The outcome of the negotiations carries significant implications for both nations, shaping the trajectory of the U.S. military involvement in Iraq and the pace at which Iraqi forces assume full responsibility for their country's security.

*This is a developing story.*

# U.S.-Iraq Status-of-Forces Agreement Negotiations Reach Critical Phase

## Baghdad Talks Intensify Over Troop Withdrawal Timeline and Legal Immunity Provisions

*2008*

---

Negotiations between Washington and Baghdad over a Status-of-Forces Agreement (SOFA) that would govern the presence of American troops in Iraq have entered a decisive and contentious stage, as both governments seek to establish a legal framework to replace the United Nations mandate set to expire at the end of the year.

The proposed agreement, which would define the terms under which roughly 140,000 U.S. troops operate on Iraqi soil, has become a flashpoint for Iraqi political factions, sovereignty concerns, and regional anxieties.

### The Withdrawal Timeline

A central pillar of the negotiations concerns the timeline for American military withdrawal. Iraqi negotiators, backed by Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki's government, have pressed for specific dates rather than the conditions-based framework favored by the Bush administration.

Key points under discussion include:

- **Withdrawal from cities:** Provisions calling for U.S. combat forces to pull back from Iraqi urban centers and towns, with proposals targeting mid-2009 for this initial repositioning.
- **Full withdrawal deadline:** Iraqi officials have advocated for the removal of all U.S. forces by the end of 2011, a demand that reflects growing domestic pressure to assert national sovereignty.

The Bush administration, which had long resisted what it termed "artificial timetables," gradually softened its position, with officials referring instead to "aspirational goals" and "time horizons" for troop reductions.

### Disputes Over Legal Jurisdiction

Perhaps the most sensitive issue in the negotiations concerns legal jurisdiction over American personnel—a matter touching directly on questions of Iraqi sovereignty.

**Iraqi demands** centered on securing the right to prosecute U.S. soldiers and private contractors for serious crimes committed off-duty and outside military installations. The issue of contractor immunity gained particular urgency following incidents involving private security firms.

**U.S. concerns** revolved around protecting service members from prosecution in the Iraqi judicial system, with the Pentagon insisting that American troops remain subject primarily to U.S. military law.

Negotiators worked toward compromise language that would grant Iraq limited jurisdiction under narrowly defined circumstances, while preserving broad immunities for troops acting within the scope of their duties. The distinction between on-duty and off-duty conduct, and between actions on and off base, proved especially difficult to resolve.

### Opposition from the Sadrist Movement

The negotiations have galvanized fierce opposition from the movement led by Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, whose followers view any agreement legitimizing a continued American presence as an affront to Iraqi independence.

Sadr's movement mobilized in several ways:

- **Mass demonstrations:** Followers organized large Friday protests in Baghdad's Sadr City and other strongholds, with demonstrators chanting anti-American slogans and burning symbolic representations of the agreement.
- **Political pressure:** Sadrist lawmakers in parliament vowed to reject any deal, framing their opposition as a defense of national sovereignty.
- **Religious framing:** Sadr and allied clerics characterized the agreement in terms of occupation and foreign domination, calling on Iraqis to resist its ratification.

The Sadrist bloc's opposition posed a significant challenge to Maliki, complicating the government's ability to secure the parliamentary approval required to enact the agreement.

### Broader Political Context

Beyond the Sadrists, the negotiations unfolded amid a complex web of competing interests. Iran was widely reported to oppose the agreement and to exert influence among Iraqi Shiite factions. Meanwhile, Iraq's Sunni and Kurdish blocs weighed their own positions, and Grand Ayatollah Ali al-Sistani signaled that any agreement should command broad national consensus and protect Iraqi interests.

The Maliki government faced the delicate task of negotiating terms acceptable to Washington while satisfying domestic constituencies wary of perpetuating a foreign military presence.

### Looking Ahead

With the U.N. mandate's expiration looming, both governments faced pressure to finalize an agreement or seek alternative arrangements. The outcome carried implications not only for the immediate legal status of American forces but for the trajectory of the broader U.S. military commitment in Iraq and the future of bilateral relations between the two nations.

---

# Iraqi Government Announces Proposed Amendments to U.S. Security Pact

**BAGHDAD** — Iraqi government spokesman Ali al-Dabbagh announced Tuesday that the Iraqi cabinet had approved a series of amendments to the proposed security agreement governing the presence of U.S. forces in the country, setting the stage for what officials described as intensive renewed negotiations with Washington.

Speaking at a press conference in the heavily fortified Green Zone, al-Dabbagh said the amendments reflected concerns raised by Iraqi political blocs and religious leaders who had expressed reservations about the original draft.

"These amendments represent the will of the Iraqi people and are necessary to protect Iraqi sovereignty," al-Dabbagh told reporters. "We are seeking a partnership based on mutual respect and clear timelines."

The proposed changes reportedly include firmer language on the withdrawal of American troops, greater Iraqi jurisdiction over U.S. personnel accused of serious crimes, and tighter restrictions on the use of Iraqi territory for launching operations against neighboring countries.

## U.S. Response Measured but Cautious

American officials responded cautiously to the announcement. A spokesman for the U.S. Embassy in Baghdad said Washington was "reviewing the proposed amendments carefully" but declined to comment on specific provisions.

"We remain committed to reaching an agreement that serves the interests of both nations," the spokesman said. "However, any final text must be workable for both parties."

Privately, some U.S. officials expressed concern that reopening negotiated language could delay ratification and complicate the legal framework needed to keep American forces operating in Iraq.

## Students Voice Divided Opinions

At Baghdad University, students offered mixed reactions to the news.

"This is a good step," said Mustafa Karim, a 21-year-old engineering student. "We want the Americans to leave eventually, but we also need stability. If these amendments protect our sovereignty, then they are welcome."

Others remained skeptical. "Amendments on paper mean nothing if they are not enforced," said Layla Hassan, a law student. "We have heard many promises before."

A third student, Ahmed Jabbar, said he worried about the security vacuum a hasty withdrawal might create. "I want them gone, but not before our own forces are ready," he said.

The proposed amendments now return to negotiators, with both governments facing pressure to finalize the agreement before existing arrangements expire.

# Iraqi Law Students Protest as U.S. Troop Agreement Sparks Jurisdiction Dispute

**BAGHDAD** — Hundreds of law students demonstrated at Mustansiriya University on Tuesday, adding their voices to a growing chorus of Iraqi opposition to a proposed security agreement that would govern the presence of American forces in the country, with the question of legal jurisdiction over U.S. troops emerging as the most contentious sticking point.

The status-of-forces agreement, under negotiation between Baghdad and Washington, would establish the legal framework for American military operations after the United Nations mandate authorizing the troop presence expires at the end of the year. But the talks have stalled repeatedly over Iraqi demands that U.S. soldiers be subject to Iraqi law for crimes committed off-base and off-duty.

"We are studying to become lawyers, to uphold the rule of law in our own country," said Fatima al-Rubaie, a third-year law student who helped organize the demonstration. "How can we accept an agreement that says foreign soldiers who kill Iraqis cannot be tried in Iraqi courts? This is not sovereignty. This is occupation with a signature."

The students, some carrying hand-painted banners reading "Justice Has No Immunity," gathered in the university courtyard before marching to the main gate, where they were met by university security and a small contingent of Iraqi police. The demonstration remained peaceful.

## Core Disagreement

At the heart of the dispute is the doctrine of jurisdiction — specifically, which nation's courts would have the authority to prosecute American service members accused of crimes against Iraqi civilians.

U.S. negotiators have pressed for broad immunity for American personnel, consistent with arrangements Washington maintains in dozens of countries where its forces are stationed. Iraqi officials, facing intense public and parliamentary pressure, have insisted that immunity cannot extend to serious crimes committed outside the scope of official duties.

"The Iraqi position reflects a fundamental principle recognized in international law — that a sovereign state exercises jurisdiction over acts committed on its territory," said Dr. Nabil Hassan, a professor of international law at Mustansiriya who addressed the students briefly during the protest. "The American demand for total immunity would create a category of persons who stand above the law. No self-respecting legal system can accept that."

The disagreement has taken on symbolic weight far beyond the technical language of the draft accord. For many Iraqis, the immunity granted to private security contractors under earlier Coalition Provisional Authority orders remains a raw wound, particularly following incidents in which civilians were killed with little apparent accountability.

## Political Pressure Mounts

The negotiations have exposed deep divisions within Iraq's political establishment. Several parliamentary blocs have vowed to reject any agreement that does not preserve Iraqi jurisdiction, while others warn that a failure to reach a deal could leave the country without a legal basis for the security cooperation that many officials privately concede remains necessary.

Prominent religious authorities have also weighed in, with some issuing statements insisting that any agreement must not compromise Iraqi sovereignty. Their interventions have added a powerful dimension to the debate, resonating with a population weary of foreign military presence.

"Our professors teach us that a contract signed under pressure, without equal footing, is not a just contract," said Omar Khalid, a second-year student at the protest. "We are not against Americans as people. We are against being told that our courts, our judges, our constitution mean nothing when a foreign soldier is involved."

## Washington's Position

American officials have defended their stance as standard practice, noting that troop immunity provisions are a feature of security arrangements the United States maintains worldwide. They argue that subjecting service members to unfamiliar legal systems could expose them to politically motivated prosecutions and would be unacceptable to the U.S. Congress.

U.S. representatives have signaled some willingness to compromise, reportedly floating proposals under which jurisdiction might be shared or determined case by case, depending on whether an alleged offense occurred while a service member was on duty. Iraqi negotiators have thus far found such formulas insufficient.

A spokesman for the U.S. mission, speaking on customary terms of anonymity, said negotiations were continuing "in good faith" and expressed confidence that "a mutually acceptable framework" could be reached. He declined to discuss specific provisions.

## An Uncertain Timeline

With the U.N. mandate set to lapse, both governments face mounting pressure to conclude an agreement or find an alternative arrangement. Iraqi officials have raised the possibility of seeking a temporary extension of the existing mandate should the talks fail to produce a deal in time — an option American negotiators are said to view with reluctance.

For the students at Mustansiriya, however, the debate is less about deadlines than about principle.

"We will be the lawyers and judges of tomorrow's Iraq," said al-Rubaie, the organizer, as the crowd began to disperse in the afternoon heat. "What kind of country do we inherit if the first lesson is that justice can be negotiated away?"

The university, one of the oldest and largest in Iraq, has a long history of political activism and has itself been the target of violence during the years of conflict. Tuesday's demonstration, students said, would not be the last if negotiators failed to address their concerns.

*— Additional reporting contributed from Baghdad.*
